quotes.text: The album combines elements of Experimental Rock, Avant Garde, Blues, Free Jazz, but did anyone ask if those things should be joined in to one.
An album so unconventional that it inspired countless musicians
The album has 28 songs on it…songs…I am not sure that word is accurate. There are 28 tracks on it, that might simplify it.

What I got sounded like a bunch of guys stoned off their ass, never have a played a lick of music in their life and as they walked in to a room they saw some instruments lying around haphazardly on the floor. They picked them up and each one of them started to play a song, but nobody said which song to play so they all played a different song at the same time.
There were songs with music, there were spoken word songs and there were songs that I am not sure can legally be classified as songs or even music.

He didn't seem to have a clue what he was going to say and if he messed up, he would try the line again and they would keep going. No editing, no cleaning up, just leaving it as is for all the world to hear the mistakes.
The album had no direction, no two songs were alike (which is actually pretty damn impressive)
This ain't music, it is a bunch of random noise pieced together and called art.

In that spirit the making of this album veers well into the territory of bizarre, absurd, and shocking as the entire band lived in a cultish commune for 8 months rehearsing for the 6 hour recording session. The effort and control put into this album is terrifying.

Anything that seems grainy or poor quality seems purposefully done like "The Dust Blows Forward 'N the Dust Blows Back", "China Pig", and "Orange Claw Hammer". Incidentally these songs are reminiscent of Delta blues and bluegrass recordings one would find on wax cylinders in some archive. The effects of skipping and popping actually coincide with parts of the songs and even set the rhythm.
One could argue the use of repetition is so prevalent it is nearly conceptual.

Another example of intended repetition is "The Blimp (Mousetrapreplica)" with its spoken word reminiscent of the War of the Worlds broadcast, and that places great emphasis on its subject in a way that the alarmed speaker seems absurd and humorous.

Some of the advanced music theory present were more likely found in orchestral pieces or required familiarity with blue and jazz many audiences couldn't or didn't access. Those factors make atonal songs like "Dali's Car", "Hair Pie 2", and "Pena" seem like noise.

The more avant garde songs have a core structure and everything that seems like nonsense then compliments, such as the screaming in "Pena" proves to be both a descant as well as setting the tone to the mood of the chaos described in the spoken word.

Despite a methodical chaos sometimes what seems like absurdity is a tongue-in-cheek remark. When it seems like the band goofing off in between takes is actually a combination of a fourth wall break and a slight joke about pop culture.
There is also the clumsy use of language that is probably meant to be flowery in "Old Fart at Play" that adds to the comical nature of everything in the song.

Regardless of the shortcomings found in the album as different as as this album appears to be it actually follows many forms of music theory that lead to a greater appreciation for the genius behind it.

Captain Beefheart and His Magic Band managed to fuse them together and not deny them, but it also required that frightening level of control and structure that the Incredible String Band wanted to reject.

Unlike Captain Beefheart the Incredible String Band seemed uncertain how to break away from their folk past in order to embrace more experimental and artist elements and lacked the proper team to guide them. Captain Beefheart and His Magic Band managed to fuse them together and not deny them, but it also required that frightening level of control and structure that the Incredible String Band wanted to reject.
Captain Beefheart had someone produce the album who is no stranger to the uncanny and unconventional.

After receiving an in-depth education in de bloose from Frank Zappa as a thoroughly baked Mojave teenager, Captain Beefheart brings much more than the standard "soulful" shouts and croons to his over-the-top career-best performances. He switches the microphone on and off. He sneers in that mic-destroying manner that he ripped off from Howlin' Wolf and sends his voice through a series of processing effects, looping his growls and squealing in flaming falsetto three years before Jim Morrison did the same on the end of "Cars Hiss By My Window." He plays a shehnai — a kind of Indian oboe — throughout "Tarotplane" and "25th Century Quaker."
The Magic Band, however, provides him with the near-perfect canvas for these wild explorations of tonality and meaning.

The guitarists, meanwhile, never wank off into the amelodic wanderland that ensnared aforementioned blues-rock dinosaurs — they are unexpectedly tasteful and stick mostly to the established tune. No onstage woodshedding for Jeff Cotton and Alex St. Clair. What the Magic Band actually does is far more exciting. Their cohesion enables them to play hot potato with the dynamics, bouncing off one another and giving subtle, thrilling cues to change things around, to grow louder or softer or segue into a freer section of the song.
